extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of poetics; literary critics, translators, and poets studying Aristotle's theory of epic and tragedy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting normative criteria from Aristotle's Poetics for composing and judging epic (epopee) and tragic poetry: unity, length, metre, characterization, allowable licence, and how to answer critical objections. Suited to theory-driven literary criticism and creative practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of epic subject (select a part, not the whole)
rubrics_metrics.description: He did not even attempt to describe the whole Trojan war... Taking, therefore, only one part for his subject, he introduces abundance of episodes from the other parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a single part/period/action as the epic's subject so the poem is comprehensible; adorn the main subject with episodes from other parts (e.g., catalogue of the ships) rather than attempting an encyclopaedic whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic species and shared parts with tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The species of the epopee are the same with those of tragedy. For the epopee must be either simple, complex, moral, or pathetic. The parts also are the same, except the music and the scenery. It should have peripetia, discovery, and pathos, and the language ... should be beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess epic by the same structural categories as tragedy (simple/complex/moral/pathetic), ensuring presence of peripeteia, anagnorisis (discovery), and pathos; judge language for beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and comprehensibility (epic)
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a possibility of comprehending the beginning and end in one view; and that will happen if it is a little... reduced to the same length with the number of tragedies that are formed at one time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic must be long enough to include necessary episodes but not so diffuse that the beginning and end cannot be grasped; consider a prudent moderation of length to preserve unity and reader/listener comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of episodes and variety (epic advantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: The epopee, being a narration, may introduce many parts, from which, if they relate to the principal subject, the bulk of the poem will be increased, which will add greatly to its magnificence; the hearer will be transported from place to place, and a variety of episodes may be introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce diverse episodes when they relate to and enrich the principal subject; use variety to produce grandeur and to avoid the sameness that causes satiety in tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of heroic verse
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of heroic verse has been confirmed by experience... the heroic measure excels every other kind in dignity and elevation; on which account it is most capable of receiving foreign and metaphorical expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer heroic (hexameter-style) measure for epic/narrative imitation because of its dignity and capacity for elevated/metaphorical diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing incompatible metres/modes
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be very absurd to mix them together, as was done by Chaeremon... iambics and tetrameters require the assistance of movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mix heroic narrative verse with metres that imply stage-movement (iambic, tetrameter); mixing meters that demand different modes of presentation is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet should appear as little as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should appear himself as little as possible; for whenever he speaks in his own person, he ceases to be an imitator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize the poet's intrusions and authorial commentary; let characters and actions speak the imitation rather than overt authorial presence (Homer as model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce agents with characteristic manners
rubrics_metrics.description: He produces no agent without characteristic manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters distinguished by consistent, characteristic manners—every introduced agent should be marked by identifiable behavioural traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of the marvellous/wonder
rubrics_metrics.description: Though wonder ought to be excited by tragedy, yet things contrary to reason, from which the marvellous chiefly arises, are better admitted in the epopee... In general, whatever is wonderful is pleasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The marvellous and events that strain reason are more tolerable in epic narration than onstage tragedy; use wondrous elements when they please and can be concealed or justified by the narrative mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer probable impossibility to improbable possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: He also teaches us to prefer impossible circumstances, if they are probable, to possible ones that are improbable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing between alternatives, prefer an impossible-seeming event that accords with probability/common belief over a technically possible but unlikely event—probability of acceptance matters more than strict possibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confine or conceal absurdities outside the action
rubrics_metrics.description: If it cannot be avoided, it should at least be confined to circumstances out of the action itself... it is ridiculous to say that otherwise the fables would be destroyed, for such fables should not at first be formed; but if they are so formed, it seems most reasonable to hide the absurdity as much as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If absurd elements are necessary, place them outside central action (e.g., ignorance of a fact by a character) or conceal them in the narration to reduce their disruptive effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour language in connective/uninteresting parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The language ought particularly to be laboured in those uninterested parts which are neither moral nor sentimental; for the manners and sentiment are obscured by too splendid a diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polish diction especially in connective passages where the poet speaks in his own person; avoid overly splendid diction where character and sentiment should be clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specious fallacies / false reasoning for effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Homer also was the best instructor how to introduce specious fallacies by means of false reasoning. For men are apt to imagine...so, if the latter circumstance be false, they conclude improperly that the former is so too: but it does not follow...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategically employ plausible but fallacious reasoning in characters to produce believable error, suspense, or dramatic effect—use human cognitive tendencies to enrich narrative/characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of poetic error (inherent vs accidental)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two sorts of error to which poetry is liable, one proceeding from itself, the other from accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish faults that arise from poetic art or incompetence from those due to external accident or ignorance in another non-poetic technical art; errors intrinsic to the poet's craft are more blameworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error: impossible according to another art
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet errs, if what he writes is impossible according to the rules of the art he treats of; but he may be excused, if he attains his purposed end by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid writing impossibilities that violate the technical rules of a represented discipline (e.g., medicine, horsemanship); if included, justify them by demonstrable poetic purpose or necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excuse for error if it attains poetical end
rubrics_metrics.description: He may be excused, if he attains his purposed end by it, viz. if he renders that, or any other part of the poem more interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An otherwise faulty description may be permissible when it serves to enhance interest, character, or the poem's end—still prefer solutions that avoid violating technical rules where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of imitation (what/how to represent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must either draw things as they were or are, or as they are said or imagined to be, or as they ought to be. And he must form these imitations either by plain language, or by words and metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to depict reality, popular belief, or idealized 'ought-to-be' and whether to use plain exposition or figurative/metaphorical language; consistency with chosen mode matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections of criticism: five species
rubrics_metrics.description: The objections of criticism may then be reduced to the these five species: the impossible, the absurd, the hurtful, the contradictory, and the errors against the rules of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When answering criticism, classify objections into these five types to target appropriate responses or remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering objections — I: poem makes it more interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: I. If the poem is made more interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An element objected to may be excused if its inclusion demonstrably increases the poem's interest or overall effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering objections — II: error due to ignorance in particular art
rubrics_metrics.description: II. If the poet errs from ignorance in any particular art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a misstatement arises from genuine lack of technical knowledge in a non-poetic art, this may mitigate blame—distinguish between technical and poetic competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering objections — III: describes things as they ought to be
rubrics_metrics.description: III. If, instead of describing things as they are, he describes them as they ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depicting idealized or exemplary versions of people/things (how they ought to be) can legitimately justify departures from literal truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering objections — IV: according to received opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: IV. Or according to received opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the depiction accords with common or traditional beliefs, it may be excused even if not strictly factual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering objections — V: as they actually were at the time
rubrics_metrics.description: V. Or as they actually were at the time the events are supposed to have happened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical or customary practices of the period depicted can justify representations that seem odd now.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering objections — VI: according to circumstances of time/place/character
rubrics_metrics.description: VI. Or according to the circumstances of time and place, and the character of the speaker or actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess statements/actions in light of who speaks, to whom, why, when, and where; propriety depends on context and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering objections — VII: by use of foreign words
rubrics_metrics.description: VII. Or by the use of foreign words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign/localized diction can account for apparently odd expressions; interpret awkwardness as dialectal or foreign usage where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering objections — VIII: by metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: VIII. Or by metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent improprieties may be figurative; consider metaphorical reading before condemning diction or imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering objections — IX: by accent (prosody)
rubrics_metrics.description: IX. Or by the accent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosodic/accidental differences (accent, stress) may change sense; check ancient pronunciations/accents in contested lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering objections — X: by division of the sentence (punctuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: X. Or by the division of the sentence, i.e., the punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different punctuation or sentence division can produce different readings; re-punctuate to resolve ambiguities before faulting the poet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering objections — XI: by ambiguous/different meanings of a word
rubrics_metrics.description: XI. Or by the different and ambiguous meanings a word may have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate polysemy: a contested line may be resolved by choosing a different but legitimate sense of a word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering objections — XII: by error of the objector
rubrics_metrics.description: XII. Or by the error of the objector, who first takes up an opinion without foundation, and then blames the poet for saying what may not agree with that opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the critic's own mistaken presuppositions generate the objection; sometimes the blame lies with the objector's false premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider character and circumstances in judging propriety
rubrics_metrics.description: When examining whether a thing is either said or done properly or improperly, we are not only to regard whether the thing itself is good or bad, but we must consider the character of the actor or speaker, as well as concerning whom, and to whom, and for what cause, he speaks or acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always evaluate utterances/actions relative to the speaker's character, audience, and motive; what is proper for one character may be improper for another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy preferred for concentrated effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy... has every requisite in common with the epopee... with the additional ornaments of music and scenery... It is, therefore, affecting, both, when it is read and acted. And it possesses another advantage, in having the period of its duration confined to a shorter space... being, as it were, condensed, it is more agreeable than if it were protracted through a longer succession of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tragic works for their concentrated unity and condensed time-frame; tragedy often attains its end more effectually because of its brevity and concentrated structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic has less unity but greater magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The epic imitation has less unity, since there is no epic poem that cannot furnish subjects for several tragedies... the epopee possesses many things which contribute greatly to extend its length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that epic can embrace multiple episodes and larger scope; judge unity with attention to how the epic binds its parts to the principal action.
